description:
Two-person team forming for "Flame in Freefall": one software engineer (Python, FastAPI, WebGL) and one medical student (MBBS) : pairing the physics/AI side with the crew-health side: smoke toxicity, human factors, medical response in microgravity.

Plan: a fire-safety simulator for spacecraft habitats, built on real NASA combustion data.
summary:
Fire behaves very differently in orbit. Without buoyancy, flames become dim spherical diffusion flames that spread slowly and burn less completely, so ground flammability tests can mislead and, in a sealed module, toxic smoke can threaten a crew before heat does.

Ashes of Microgravity is an open-source, flight-calibrated fire-safety lab that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA microgravity combustion findings in milliseconds. It couples (1) a reduced-order flame-spread model and a 2D thermal-pyrolysis solver calibrated on 13 NASA Saffire and BASS-II flight runs, (2) a cabin toxicology model using NASA SMAC limits, ISO 13571 exposure dose and carboxyhemoglobin kinetics, (3) a fast neural emulator, and (4) a citation-grounded assistant over NASA reports. It compares 118 aerospace materials across ISS, Moon, Mars and Earth gravity, with uncertainty and applicability reported for every result.

The live demo runs in lite mode (physics + 2D PDE + toxicology) due to the 512 MB RAM limit of free hosting; the AI emulator and RAG literature assistant are reproducible via the included Dockerfile on any 2 GB+ platform.

We also report accuracy honestly: about 10-12% error under fully nested leave-one-out validation, with limitations documented. It is a research and screening tool, not a certification or medical system.
details:
THE PROBLEM

On Earth, hot gases rise and feed a flame. In orbit there is no buoyancy: flames become dim, spherical diffusion flames governed by diffusion and cabin airflow, spread slowly, burn less completely, and fill a sealed module with CO, soot and acid gases. Ground flammability tests (NASA-STD-6001) can therefore mislead, and decades of NASA microgravity combustion results (Saffire, BASS-II, SoFIE) sit in reports that engineers cannot query quickly.

WHAT IT DOES

Ashes of Microgravity is an interactive open-source lab (web UI + REST API):

- Summarize: a citation-grounded literature assistant over 3,426 passages from NASA Saffire, BASS-II and SoFIE reports, with an offline fallback.

- Rank: compares up to 118 aerospace materials at ISS (0g), Moon (0.16g), Mars (0.38g) and Earth (1g), ranking by predicted flame-spread rate and 10-minute cabin toxicity hazard.

- Interpret: a physics-grounded insight engine explains why a flame spreads or extinguishes (thermal regime, heat balance, ventilation) and gives screening-level guidance.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Physics engine: reduced-order flame spread (de Ris / Quintiere heat balance, Stefan-Boltzmann losses, char insulation, quasi-2D edge effects) plus a 2D thermal-pyrolysis PDE solver resolving parabolic vs concave flame fronts.

2. Crew toxicology: well-mixed cabin ODE with ECLSS scrubbing, species yields (SFPE/Tewarson), NASA SMAC limits (JSC 20584), ISO 13571 fractional effective dose, and carboxyhemoglobin uptake with oxygen-mask washout.

3. Neural emulator: a 41-feature, 5-model PyTorch ensemble that reproduces the physics engine in about 2 ms and reports ensemble disagreement. The physics engine always stays authoritative.

4. Every result carries first-order uncertainty and an applicability score (distance from the flight-validated envelope).

VALIDITY

The physics is calibrated on 13 flight runs (NASA Saffire I-V, BASS-II); in-sample error is 5.9%. Because 13 points can be overfit, we ran fully nested leave-one-out validation (all 16 empirical constants refit in every fold): 10.4-12.3% MAPE across three optimiser seeds. Leave-one-mission-out is less stable (8-20%). We publish which constants the data cannot identify, and the emulator's error against the physics engine (about 2% on plates and fabrics, up to 26% on low-flow PMMA rods). 56 automated tests pass. Only 3 of the 118 materials have flight data; the rest are extrapolations with lower applicability scores.

IMPACT

Fast screening for material selection and Moon/Mars habitat planning, a teaching tool for why microgravity fire safety differs, and open validation scripts that make the model's limits transparent for follow-up research.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, PyTorch, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers, Groq-hosted LLM (optional, for the literature assistant), WebGL front end, Docker, GitHub Actions.

CREATIVITY

Couples combustion physics with crew physiology (built by a CS/data-science student and an MBBS student): a microgravity fire is judged by whether people survive, not only whether flames spread. AI is kept honest: physics is authoritative, the emulator is flagged when it diverges, and claims are traceable.

LIMITATIONS

Research and screening tool: not NASA-STD-6001 certification and not medical advice. Toxicology is not validated against real exposure data and assumes a well-mixed cabin.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Honourable mentions to @gemini @claude and @chatgpt for helping throughout this project. They were used for debugging, writing some code, voice-over, guidance, and review.
